Extraction: Surveying Root Cause Analysis Techniques: A Comprehensive Review of Aspects for Multi-Service Applications
Zhijing Li; Jianbo Yu; Zhijun Huang; Yusheng Huang
2026 (accepted 8 November 2025; published 13 November 2025); IEEE Transactions on Services Computing (TSC), Vol. 19, No. 1, January/February 2026

Root Cause Analysis (RCA) techniques remain "highly fragmented, often developed for isolated domains and lacking integration across multi-service environments"; complex interdependencies among monitoring components in distributed, microservice, and cloud-based systems make identifying the root cause of failures a crucial but difficult operation and maintenance task (Sec. I, p. 808-809)

Not a proposed system but a survey: it organizes RCA methods along two orthogonal axes - application scenarios (cloud services, microservices, industrial systems) and input-data types (logs, traces, metrics, reports) - and synthesizes algorithmic families, hybrid/LLM approaches, datasets, tools, and evaluation metrics (Abstract; Sec. I, p. 808-809); regarding agentic AI, it reviews LLM-based RCA: fine-tuned GPT-3.x inferring root causes and fixes from 40K+ Microsoft incident summaries [64], a ReAct-based LLM agent retrieving logs, metrics, and incident tickets for out-of-distribution RCA [65], and the OpenRCA benchmark for LLM agents [66] (Sec. VII, p. 815)

Systematic literature review following Kitchenham et al. guidelines; structured keyword search across five databases (Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, DBLP, Scopus); 96 keyword-venue combination queries via an automated crawler; studies published 2017-2025; 845 papers collected, 97 peer-reviewed studies selected after inclusion/exclusion criteria; graph-based analysis used to map research connections (Sec. II, p. 809-810)

Not specified as MTTD/MTTR values; only a qualitative claim that log analysis "can be found quickly, leading to a faster time to identify and fix problems" (Sec. III.B, p. 811); the survey's reviewed evaluation metrics are Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-Score, Top@N (e.g., AC@k, PR@k, HR@k), MRR, runtime, FP/FN, and clustering metrics - not detection/recovery time metrics (Sec. X, p. 820-822)

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: Reports third-party results: fine-tuned LLMs "surpass encoder-decoder baselines in generating effective explanations and mitigation plans" on 40K+ Microsoft incidents [64]; a ReAct-based LLM agent matches strong baselines with higher factual accuracy, while post-mortem comments offer no added benefit [65]; on the OpenRCA benchmark (335 failures, 68 GB telemetry) "even the best LLM agent solves only 11.3% of cases" [66]; LLM-based methods are "constrained by limited context, susceptibility to hallucinations, and low real-world success rates" (Sec. VII, p. 815; Sec. XII, p. 822)

Authors acknowledge their 96 keyword+venue search "may have excluded valuable work from other venues" and call for including gray literature (Sec. XIII, p. 823); open issues: algorithmic limitations (correlation/heuristic methods fail to capture true causality; lack of interpretability), scarcity of large-scale, realistic, multi-modal RCA datasets, and poor cross-domain generalization; future work: improved LLM contextual understanding and reduced hallucinations, multimodal telemetry fusion (logs, traces, metrics, topology), and explainable real-time RCA tools with causal reasoning and streaming inference (Sec. XII, p. 822-823)

This survey maps the RCA landscape that an Agentic AI incident-response copilot must operate in, organizing techniques by telemetry input (logs, traces, metrics, reports) and scenario (cloud, microservices) - directly matching the observability data a copilot would consume to reduce MTTD/MTTR. Its Section VII on hybrid and LLM-based RCA, especially the ReAct agent study and the OpenRCA finding that the best LLM agent solves only 11.3% of cases, provides sobering baseline evidence for the feasibility claims of my thesis. Its consolidated inventory of public/industrial datasets (e.g., TrainTicket, Sock Shop, HDFS) and evaluation metrics (Top@N, MRR) is directly reusable for designing my experimental evaluation. However, it offers no MTTD/MTTR measurements, so it serves as background and gap evidence rather than a metric baseline.

Medium - it is an adjacent AIOps/RCA survey covering LLM-agent approaches and observability data highly relevant to an incident-response copilot, but it does not measure MTTD/MTTR with an agentic approach.
